title: The thousandth lotus
hookLine: Vishnu, one lotus short, offers his own eye; why the flower on the shrine stands for the one who offers it
carry: the flower stands for your heart
last: DEEPA — THE LAMP'S LIGHT IS GREETED AS GOD.

lines: A THOUSAND NAMES, A THOUSAND LOTUSES.
cards: The gods were losing to the demons, and Vishnu went to Shiva's mountain to ask for help. He didn't come empty-handed. He brought a thousand lotuses, one for each of Shiva's thousand names, and began: a name, a flower.
A name, a flower. Shiva watched, and decided to test him. Quietly, he hid one lotus.
Nine hundred and ninety-nine names in, Vishnu reached into the basket, and it was empty. He didn't stop the prayer. He didn't send anyone to find another flower.
People call Vishnu lotus-eyed. So he got ready to offer his own eye.

teach.b: Shiva stopped him, deeply moved, and gave Vishnu the shining discus he carries ever since, the Sudarshana. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it. Look at what the story says a flower is.
When the basket ran out, Vishnu didn't see a missing decoration. He saw a gap only he could fill, because the flower had been standing in for him the whole time.

teach.h: BHAKTI: THE FLOWER STANDS FOR YOU.
teach.b: That's the heart of bhakti, devotion, the path of love: in puja, the flower is a stand-in for the one who offers it.
Krishna says the same thing another way: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, and I accept it. The price doesn't matter. The heart does.
So a shrine flower comes with small habits.
It's picked fresh for the morning, and yesterday's is taken down. One that fell on the floor is usually not offered. It's often left unsmelled, because the first enjoyment isn't the giver's.
Different forms of God have favorites: red hibiscus for Ganesha and the Goddess, bilva leaves for Shiva, tulsi for Vishnu and Krishna.

teach.h: A NEW ONE TOMORROW, LIKE YOU.
teach.b: And by evening it droops, so tomorrow you bring a new one, the way you bring yourself again. Many teachers read it simply: the flower on the plate is really you. So a silk flower can sit there all year, and it's pretty.
It just can't stand in for anyone.

how: Many Hindus place fresh flowers at the home shrine each morning as an offering of devotion (bhakti), taking down the previous day's, usually not offering a fallen flower or smelling one meant for the shrine, and often choosing flowers or leaves dear to a particular deity, such as hibiscus for Ganesha, bilva for Shiva and tulsi for Vishnu or Krishna.

o: a garland worn by a new bride
an incense stick lit at the shrine
a fresh flower offered in puja

games.q: the thousandth lotus — tap the pairs.
p: a lotus for each of Shiva's thousand names
hid one lotus to test him
Vishnu ready to offer his own eye

s: when one lotus was missing, Vishnu stopped the prayer
he was ready to offer his own eye, because the flower stood for him all along.
in bhakti, the flower on the plate stands for the one who offers it
many teachers read it that way: the flower is really you.
Krishna says only costly offerings are accepted
a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, given with love: the heart is what counts.

games.q: there are no flowers in the house this morning, only the tulsi pot on the windowsill. what fits today's teaching?
o: skip the offering until you can buy proper flowers.
offer one tulsi leaf with love: it stands for you just as well.
games.why: a leaf offered with love is accepted. the price was never the point; the heart behind it is, the way Vishnu's lotuses stood for Vishnu.

practice: Find a flower or a leaf near you, or picture one, and look at it closely: the color, the veins, the edge that won't look like this tomorrow.

Set it down somewhere that matters to you, your corner, a windowsill, beside a photo of someone you love. If you pray, offer it with a name you honor, Om namah shivaya, or Krishna's name, and let it carry you with it.
If you don't pray, name one thing you're bringing with it today, and sit with it.

wordCard.voice: Pushpa. The flower: picked fresh, left unsmelled, and offered in your place, the way Vishnu's lotuses were.

orig.note: Sanskrit puṣpa: flower. One of the classic offerings of puja.

carryVoice: Your line: the flower stands for your heart. Vishnu was ready to give himself when the flowers ran out. That's day one hundred thirteen.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Kotirudra Samhita (Vishnu worships Shiva with a thousand lotuses and the thousand names, offers his eye when one is missing, and receives the Sudarshana)
Bhagavad Gita 9.26 (a leaf, a flower, a fruit, water, offered with devotion)
